subject: VPC burst-control & warmup playbook for private GPU pools
messages:
From: Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>
To: Acme Eng Lead <eng-lead@acme-corp.com>, CloudIntegrator Ops <ops@cloudintegrator.io>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-04-01T09:14:00-07:00
Subject: VPC burst-control & warmup playbook for private GPU pools

Hi Alex / team,

Thanks for the details on your expected traffic patterns for the VPC deployment. We sketched a concise playbook (attached) that focuses on two things you called out: sudden short bursts from customer-facing features, and long-tail sustained peaks during batch jobs. Key proposals:

- Warmup (prefix/cache): proactive prefix caching of the 20 most common prompts + KV cache priming using a short headless run after deploy. Expected p95 improvement for first-request latency: ~40-60% in our sim.
- Burst control / circuit breaker: token-budget based circuit breaker at the routing layer that moves low-priority requests to a cheaper model-variant when pool utilization > 80%.
- Autoscaler tuning: target scale-up trigger at 68% GPU util (avg across pool), scale-down after 4m cooldown. Use linear predictor for 30s lookahead to avoid overshoot on 5–15s spikes.

I've attached the throughput sim we ran locally. Initial numbers assume your medium L2 profile (A100-equivalent) and the standard token mix you shared. Can Marissa and Laura weigh in on runbook wording and the network checklist (MTU, RDMA/NIC bonding)?

Next step: short call with CloudIntegrator ops to align on jumbo frames and NIC-level metrics. Proposed times Thursday 10–11 PT.

Thanks,
Connor
--
Connor O'Brien
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Eng Lead <eng-lead@acme-corp.com>
To: Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>
Cc: CloudIntegrator Ops <ops@cloudintegrator.io>
Date: 2028-04-01T10:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: VPC burst-control & warmup playbook for private GPU pools

Connor, thanks — this looks immediately useful. A few clarifying Qs from my side before the call:

1) When you say "prefix caching of top 20 prompts", do you mean a deterministic cache pre-warm that lives on every GPU node, or a shared cache in front of the serving tier? Our infra prefers node-local caches to avoid cross-node network reads.

2) How tolerant is the circuit-breaker approach to preserving QoE? We can accept lower-quality fallbacks for non-critical endpoints, but anything customer-facing needs a strict p95 latency bound (target 250ms).

3) What's the expected network egress for the warmup step? We run in a constrained VPC with some inter-AZ link caps.

We can do Thu 10:30 PT for the call. I'll invite our platform lead.

— Alex

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>, Acme Eng Lead <eng-lead@acme-corp.com>, CloudIntegrator Ops <ops@cloudintegrator.io>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-04-01T13:22:00-07:00
Subject: Re: VPC burst-control & warmup playbook for private GPU pools

Alex — quick answers inline.

1) Prefix cache: we recommend a hybrid: node-local warmup + lightweight shared prefix index. Reason: node-local gives the lowest p95 for first requests; shared index reduces duplicated work for very large pools. Implementation note: the warmup run is a <5m headless pass per node that touches 200–500 tokens per prompt set. If your inter-AZ caps are tight, stick with node-local only.

2) Circuit-breaker QoE: tiered policy. Policy example:
  - Priority=high (customer-facing critical): no model-variant fallback until GPU util >= 92%. Use request queue and early drop after 2s queue time.
  - Priority=medium: fallback to the 8-bit quantized variant at util >= 80%.
  - Priority=low: immediately route to lower-cost ensemble if util >= 70%.

We calibrated these thresholds to keep p95 under 250ms for high-priority traffic in our sims; medium will see 15–25% latency increase but token cost drop of ~40%.

3) Warmup network egress: our sim shows ~120MB/node for the 20-prompt, 500-token warmup if you fetch shared artifacts (tokenized prompts & initial kv). If you run node-local warmup from local artifacts, network is negligible — mostly internal disk reads.

Also attached a short runbook draft (runbook-gpu-circuit-breaker.md) — Connor, can you add the ops play commands and the metric names for Grafana?

Thanks,
Marissa

From: Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>
To: Acme Eng Lead <eng-lead@acme-corp.com>, Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>, CloudIntegrator Ops <ops@cloudintegrator.io>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Date: 2028-04-02T08:11:00-07:00
Subject: Re: VPC burst-control & warmup playbook for private GPU pools

Alex / team — added the network checklist and test plan points below (also in the Drive link):

- NIC / MTU: recommend MTU 9000 on host + enable jumbo frames through the top-of-rack switch. Test: iperf3 between two nodes for sustained 10s windows at target concurrency.
- RDMA: only required if you expect >60% sustained cross-node KV traffic. Prefer RoCEv2 with PFC disabled in our experience unless the fabric is lossless.
- NIC bonding: active-backup for availability; LACP only if upstream supports consistent hashing for GRPC connections.
- Ingress layer: allow 128 concurrent gRPC streams per envoy worker and tune upstream idle timeouts to 90s to avoid cold-starts when sessions recycle.

Testing plan (short):
1) Synthetic spike test: 20k short user requests over 30s, measure queue length and p95.
2) Warmup verify: deploy warmup job and verify KV hit-rate >90% for the top-20 prompts within 2 minutes.
3) Failover test: force a simulated node loss and observe routing to fallback models and autoscaler reaction time.

I'll run the iperf and GRPC concurrency test on Monday and share results. Kimberly — can you draft the Grafana dashboards for these indicators (GPU util, queue length, KV hit rate, p95 by priority)?

Laura

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
To: Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>, Acme Eng Lead <eng-lead@acme-corp.com>, CloudIntegrator Ops <ops@cloudintegrator.io>
Date: 2028-04-03T13:49:00-07:00
Subject: Re: VPC burst-control & warmup playbook for private GPU pools

Looping here with the first draft dashboards and a concise runbook snippet. Files uploaded to Drive link above. Highlights:

- Grafana panels: GPU_util_avg_1m, GPU_util_p95_5m, request_queue_len, kv_cache_hit_pct_top20, p95_latency_by_priority.
- Alerting rules (examples):
  - GPU_util_avg_5m > 85% => warn; >92% => critical.
  - request_queue_len > 200 for >30s => scale-up and enable medium-priority fallback.
  - kv_cache_hit_pct_top20 < 80% for >2m => re-run warmup job.

Runbook snippet (CLI ops):
1) Trigger warmup: redwoodctl warmup --target-pool acme-vpc-1 --prompts-file top20.txt --parallel 8
2) Force fallback policy: redwoodctl policy set --pool acme-vpc-1 --priority medium --fallback quant8
3) Immediate mitigation (hot fix): redwoodctl throttle --pool acme-vpc-1 --limit 600rps --except-priority=high

We should schedule the interop call with CloudIntegrator to confirm MTU/jumbo-frame path and whether RoCEv2 is available on their fabric. Connor — can you pick the final time? I can present the dashboards and sample alerts.

-Kim
